n: After the Isaiah chapters, Nephi comments. He admits Isaiah was hard for his people to understand because they didn’t know the Jewish style of prophecy — full of poetry, symbols, and references to local places.

f.w: the manner of prophesying among the Jews
f.g: Hebrew poetic style, symbolism, and historical references.

n: Nephi deliberately did not teach his people many Jewish customs, because of the wicked practices he had seen in Jerusalem.
He writes so his people, and future readers, can know that God’s judgments come upon all nations as He said.
Isaiah’s words are plain to those with the “spirit of prophecy.” But Nephi will also give his own prophecy in plain words. He loves plainness so his people can learn.
Nephi still delights in Isaiah. Having lived in Jerusalem, he knows the Jews understand their prophets best — and others can understand too if taught their context.

f.w: after the manner of the things of the Jews
f.g: With knowledge of Jewish history, geography, and culture.

n: Nephi didn’t teach his children Jewish ways, but having lived in Jerusalem he knows the region and has told his children of God’s judgments there.
Now Nephi gives his own plain prophecy, in which no one can be misled. When Isaiah’s prophecies are fulfilled, people will know for sure.
Isaiah’s words are valuable. Nephi wrote them for his people, who will especially understand them in the last days.
Jewish generations have suffered destruction for their wickedness, but never without warning from God’s prophets first.

f.w: save it were foretold them by the prophets

n: Right after Lehi left, destruction was foretold. They hardened their hearts, and Jerusalem was destroyed except for those taken to Babylon.
By the Spirit Nephi says they will return to Jerusalem and possess their land again.
There will be wars. Then the Only Begotten of the Father — who is also the “Father of heaven and of earth” as Creator — will come in the flesh, and they will reject Him.

f.w: the Only Begotten of the Father
the Father of heaven and of earth

n: They will crucify Him; after three days in a tomb He will rise with “healing in his wings.” All who believe will be saved. Nephi has seen His day and rejoices to prophesy of Him.

f.w: for the space of three days

n: After Christ’s resurrection and appearances, Jerusalem will be destroyed again — fulfilled by the Romans in AD 70.
The Jews will be scattered among all nations. Babylon too will be destroyed, so other nations will do the scattering.

After many generations of scattering, when they come to believe in Christ and His infinite Atonement and worship the Father in His name with pure hearts, no longer awaiting another Messiah, the time will come to gather them.
The Lord will act “a second time” to restore His people, doing a “marvelous work and a wonder.” Nephi echoes both Isaiah 11 and Isaiah 29.

f.w: a marvelous work and a wonder

n: God will bring forth His words — which will judge them at the last day — to convince them that Jesus is the true Messiah. There is only one Messiah; any other will be false.

f.w: he shall bring forth his words unto them

n: The prophets said the Messiah would come six hundred years after Lehi left Jerusalem. An angel told Nephi His name: Jesus Christ, the Son of God. “Jesus” is the Greek form of Joshua, “Jehovah saves.”

f.w: his name shall be Jesus Christ

n: Nephi swears by the God who led Israel from Egypt, healed them through the brass serpent, and gave water from the rock: there is no other name under heaven by which people can be saved but Jesus Christ.

f.w: there is none other name given under heaven
cast their eyes unto the serpent

n: God promised Nephi his writings would be preserved and passed down, so the promise to Joseph — that his seed would never perish — could be fulfilled.

f.w: the promise may be fulfilled unto Joseph

n: These records will last as long as the earth, and nations that receive them will be judged by them.

A famous verse: Nephi writes to persuade people to believe in Christ and be reconciled to God, knowing “it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do.” Grace is not a reward for effort; our faithful effort is how we receive the gift Christ freely offers.

f.w: it is by grace that we are saved

f.g: Often understood as “in addition to” or “even after” all we can do — grace is always essential.

n: Though they believe in Christ, the Nephites keep the law of Moses, looking steadily forward to Christ until the law is fulfilled.

f.w: we keep the law of Moses

n: The law was given to point to Christ. It is “dead” to them as a means of salvation; they are made alive in Christ through faith. They keep it because God commanded it.

f.w: the law hath become dead unto us

n: One of the most beloved verses in the Book of Mormon: “we talk of Christ, we rejoice in Christ, we preach of Christ, we prophesy of Christ,” so their children will know where to turn for forgiveness of sins.
They teach about the law so their children will see its limits and look to the life found in Christ — and not harden their hearts when the law is fulfilled and ends.

f.w: after the law is fulfilled in Christ

n: Because the Nephites are stubborn, Nephi has spoken plainly so they can’t misunderstand. The right way is to believe in Christ and not deny Him; to deny Him is to deny the prophets and the law.

f.w: the right way is to believe in Christ

n: Christ is the Holy One of Israel. Worship Him with all your might, mind, strength, and soul, and you will never be cast out.

f.w: Christ is the Holy One of Israel
with all your might, mind, and strength

n: Until the law of Moses is fulfilled, they must keep its rites and ordinances.

f.g: The sacrifices and rituals of the law of Moses.
